profiles.name: Ada Louise Davenport Kendall
profiles.description:
Ada Louise Davenport Kendall was a member of the National Woman’s Party and one of the "Silent Sentinels" imprisoned during the 1917-1919 campaign to picket the Wilson White House for woman suffrage. (March 31, 1867 - April 14, 1950)

She was arrested on September 13, 1917 and sentenced to thirty days at the Occoquan Workhouse. A complete term would have ended about October 13, 1917, but no personal discharge record has been found.

This record previously dated her arrest to August 1917 and was filed under her husband’s name, as Mrs. Frederick W. Kendall.

profiles.name: Allan S. Broms
profiles.description: Allan S. Broms, also recorded as Allen S. Broms, was a St. Paul socialist and World War I draft resister. He was jailed for 90 days after a September 1917 antiwar-speech arrest in Two Harbors, Minnesota. After refusing draft registration, he was forced into the Army, court-martialed at Camp Dodge for refusing military service, sentenced to twenty years, and confined at Fort Leavenworth. His sentence was reduced and he was released on March 18, 1919.

profiles.name: Amedeo Lilli
profiles.description:
Amedeo Lilli was born 1894 in Acqualagna, Italy. Immigrated to the United States in 1913.

Arrested in September 1917 after an Italian anarchist “riot” during which he was shot in the shoulder by an undercover policeman. Convicted of assault, he was sentenced to twenty-five years in Wisconsin State Prison. Pardoned in 1922 on condition of deportation, he was deported February 16, 1922.

After returning to Italy he became a tailor and, according to police surveillance extending to 1932, did not resume radical political activity.

Adapted from Kenyon Zimmer, Red Scare Deportees (kenyonzimmer.com), compiled from INS deportation case files.

profiles.name: Angel Roncal
profiles.description:
Angel Roncal was born 1896 in Spain. Immigrated to the United States in 1916.

He reportedly spent time in South America before immigrating to the U.S. in 1916. 

A member of the Niagara Falls IWW branch, he was arrested in September 1918 for failing to register for the draft, with IWW literature found in his possession. After five months in jail without trial he was released in February 1919 but immediately detained for deportation. He was deported to Spain around July 1, 1920.

Adapted from Kenyon Zimmer, Red Scare Deportees (kenyonzimmer.com), compiled from INS deportation case files.

profiles.name: Anna Gvinter
profiles.description:
Anna Gvinter was born about 1891 and was a member of the National Woman’s Party and one of the "Silent Sentinels" imprisoned during the 1917-1919 campaign to picket the Wilson White House for woman suffrage. Her exact dates of birth and death are unresolved. (printed as Anna Gwinter and by Irwin as Eleanor Gwinter)

The sources disagree about which arrest her thirty-day sentence belongs to. The better-supported chronology has her arrested on September 13, 1917 and sentenced to thirty days at the Occoquan Workhouse: she wrote from the workhouse on September 21, and an affidavit dated October 13 is consistent with release by then. Stevens’s appendix instead attaches the thirty days to the November 10 arrests, but Irwin’s November 10 list does not include her. This record follows the September chronology; original court records would be needed for certainty.

profiles.name: Carl Voss
profiles.description:
Carl Voss was born 1891 in Hamburg, Germany. Immigrated to the United States in 1910.

Born 1891, Hamburg, Germany. Sailor; laborer. Migrated to US 1910 (deserted ship). Joined the IWW 1913; 1918 became organizer for the IWW’s Metal Mine Workers’ Industrial Union No. 800. Also a member of the International Seamen’s Union. Arrested Tucson, Arizona, September 8, 1918 for failing to register for the draft; January 1919 sentenced a year in the Yavapai County Jail; reported by the sherif to have “caused him more trouble than any other prisoner he as had in jail…on account of attempting to incite riots on several occasions, and attempting to effect a jail delivery.” Arrested upon his release in January 1920 and held for deportation. Deported May 22, 1920. Subsequent activities unknown.

INS file 54860/699

See also: Harry Weinberger Papers, Yale University

Adapted from Kenyon Zimmer, Red Scare Deportees (kenyonzimmer.com), compiled from INS deportation case files.

profiles.name: Charles T. Schenck
profiles.description: Charles T. Schenck was the general Secretary of the Socialist Party of Philadelphia. In August 1917 the local printed ~15, 000 antidraft leaflets ("Long Live the Constitution... Wake Up, America!") urging draftees to assert their Thirteenth Amendment rights. Arrested in a raid on the SP Philadelphia office, convicted in late 1917. His unanimous SCOTUS appeal produced Schenck v. United States, 249 U.S. 47 (1919) — Justice Holmes's landmark "clear and present danger" / "fire in a crowded theatre" dictum. Served six months in federal prison.

profiles.name: George Polevoy
profiles.description:
George Polevoy was born 1883 in Chernihiv, Russia (present-day Ukraine). Immigrated to the United States in 1907.

Married with a child in the United States, he joined the IWW around 1914 in Moundsville, West Virginia, and also belonged to the United Mine Workers. Participated in miners’ strikes protesting the conviction of Tom Mooney and the imprisonment of Eugene V. Debs. Arrested June 1918 for disturbing the peace during a dispute with UMW leaders and sentenced to a $50 fine and ten days in jail; a union witness described him as a leader “of the foreign element…they have made all kinds of trouble.” Arrested again August 1919 and described by an immigration agent as “exceptionally shrewd and astute.” Deported to Russia February 1, 1921.

Adapted from Kenyon Zimmer, Red Scare Deportees (kenyonzimmer.com), compiled from INS deportation case files.

profiles.name: Irma Sanchini
profiles.description:
Irma Sanchini was born 1895 in Tonco, Piedmont, Italy. Immigrated to the United States in 1907.

Migrated to the United States with her father and settled in New Britain, Connecticut, where she became associated with Luigi Galleani’s anarchist circle and distributed Cronaca Sovversiva. Married Giobbe Sanchini in 1913. Arrested September 8, 1917 for helping to organize a defense fund for Galleani, she was released when the warrant was canceled but rearrested May 16, 1918. Some newspapers dubbed her the “Queen of the Anarchists,” and the district attorney hyperbolically claimed she “accomplished untold mischief in the period that she has resided in Connecticut. She is highly intelligent, very resourceful, and is considered to be much more dangerous than her husband.” Asked by an immigration agent what she thought an anarchist was, she replied, “a good man.” Deported June 24, 1919 with her husband and children. 

Reportedly suffering from tuberculosis at the time of her deportation, she died in childbirth in 1925.

Adapted from Kenyon Zimmer, Red Scare Deportees (kenyonzimmer.com), compiled from INS deportation case files.

profiles.name: John Charles Hicke
profiles.description:
John Charles Hicke was born 1882 in Bukovina, Austria-Hungary (present-day Romania). Immigrated to the United States in 1913.

Arrested in April 1918 in Oxford, Mississippi, and interned as an alien enemy at Fort Oglethorpe, Georgia, where he remained for nearly two years before being transferred to immigration custody. During detention, Hicke declared: “I am opposed to the Government of the United States and its peoples. I do not think its peoples are intelligent enough to govern themselves…I think the government should be overthrown and to accomplish this end every action would be justified.” Later, however, he claimed these statements were a strategy to expedite his deportation. He repeatedly petitioned U.S. and Austrian officials to hasten his removal. Deported to Romania on June 29, 1920.

Adapted from Kenyon Zimmer, Red Scare Deportees (kenyonzimmer.com), compiled from INS deportation case files.

profiles.name: José Ángel Hernández
profiles.description:
José Ángel Hernández was born 1885 in Tepic, Mexico.

By 1906 he was living in Los Angeles, where he became a member of the PLM-affiliated Grupo Reforma, Libertad y Justicia. By 1911 he was in Houston, Texas, serving as head of the PLM-affiliated Grupo Regeneración Solidaridad Obrera. He joined the IWW in 1913. In 1914 he married fellow PLM member Elisa Alemán, and their daughter Emancipación was born later that year. In 1915 he became an organizer for the Socialist Party’s Land League of Texas and was active in the PLM-affiliated Grupo Germinal in San Antonio. A second daughter, Susana, was born in 1916, after which Hernández separated from Alemán. In 1917 he was active in the Grupo Solidaridad in Houston and founded a mixed local of the IWW there, serving as its secretary. Arrested on August 22, 1917, for IWW organizing and illegally deported to Mexico on August 31, 1917, by an agent of the Bureau of Investigation.

Back in Mexico, Hernández was active with the IWW and the Casa del Obrero Mundial in Tampico ,and joined the anarchist Hermanos Rojos, becoming a regular contributor to their paper Germinal. In January 1918 he was elected general secretary of the Casa del Obrero Mundial in Tampico, though by March he was no longer affiliated with Hermanos Rojos. He cofounded and edited the newspaper Fuerza y Cerebro and was arrested in August 1918 for his organizing activities. In 1919 began writing for the anarchist newspaper Luz! and was arrested again as a leader of an oil workers’ strike in Tampico. In March 1920 he founded the Liga Socialista in Tampico, which endorsed electoral participation. Arrested 1921 for assisting with an IWW strike and later accused of mismanaging funds raised for a publication project. He subsequently disappeared, with some rumors suggesting he traveled to Soviet Russia.

Adapted from Kenyon Zimmer, Red Scare Deportees (kenyonzimmer.com), compiled from INS deportation case files.

profiles.name: Joseph Pass
profiles.description: Joseph Pass was a writer from New York, New York. Joseph Pass was arrested in New York City in October 1917 for " pro-peace " activity and sentenced to two years in prison. He served in McNeil Island Penitentiary. After prison Pass served on the National Committee of the International Labor Defense and from 1936 to 1943 was editor of Fight, a newspaper published by the American League Against War and Fascism. In the 1950s and 1960s Pass was subjected to surveillance by the FBI, which used agents and informants to keep tabs on him. After determining that the " subject " was a "writer by profession, " they recommended against interviewing him because he " might cause embarrassment to the Bureau " in his publications.

profiles.name: Paul Sandargos
profiles.description: Paul Sandargos was a coal miner from Scran ton, Pennsylvania. Paul Sandargos was convicted for distributing literature against the draft and sentenced to three years in prison. He served in Atlanta Penitentiary from October 17, 1917, to February 21, 1920. Sandargos had a wife and two children. In a letter to his brother, Sandargos described his meeting with Eugene Debs in prison: I see E. V. Debs on Saturday and Sunday afternoons when we are in the yard. I find him a splendid fellow and full of spirit. He will always fight for the workers, no matter where or when. All of the poor fellows here run to him for help. It is pitiful, yet funny to see men from up in the mountains who never saw or heard of him before, going to him for advice. He pats them on the shoulder and cheers them up. Says all will come out all right. That they must not wony but keep their spirits and a cool head and before long they are satisfied that being in prison with him is just as good as being outside without him. It is truly wonderful.

profiles.name: Risley W. Young
profiles.description: Rosley W. Young was one of the thirteen soldiers of the all-Black 24th Infantry Regiment hanged at Camp Travis, near San Antonio, at dawn on 11 December 1917, after the first Houston-riot court-martial (the "Nesbit case"). The executions were carried out in secret, within a day of sentencing and without the War Department review that would normally have allowed an appeal. The Houston riot of 1917 (the Camp Logan mutiny) erupted on 23 August 1917 after Houston police, enforcing Jim Crow, beat and arrested soldiers of the all-Black 24th Infantry Regiment. About 150 soldiers marched on the city; the night left some twenty people dead. In the largest court-martial in U.S. history, 118 men were tried, 19 executed, and 63 sentenced to life imprisonment. In 2023 the U.S. Army set aside all 110 convictions and honorably discharged the soldiers. (Recorded as Private Rosley W. Young)

" His name was removed from that list in 1945 when the FBI determined that the "subject is not actively engaged in un-American activities."
